frictionVectors.title: European gas dependence
frictionVectors.details: Algeria is using long-term gas contracts and pipeline access to strengthen bargaining power with Europe. Pricing, contract terms, and infrastructure investment remain points of friction.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara and regional rivalry
frictionVectors.details: Algeria's support for Western Sahara self-determination sustains tension with Morocco and complicates regional trade and energy coordination.

frictionVectors.title: External control of hydrocarbons
frictionVectors.details: International oil companies and foreign lenders retain major influence over production, technology, and revenue flows. Declining output increases pressure to offer more favorable terms.

frictionVectors.title: Lobito corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: US and European backing for the corridor is expanding Angola's strategic options, but also exposes the country to competition over access to Congolese and Zambian critical minerals.

frictionVectors.title: Cotonou port dependency
frictionVectors.details: Benin's trade and revenue position depends heavily on port infrastructure and cross-border commerce, leaving it exposed to external logistics operators and shifting regional regulations.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel spillover
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity along the northern frontier is increasing demand for foreign security assistance and border infrastructure. Instability in Niger and Burkina Faso also threatens transport and agricultural corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Diamond-market concentration
frictionVectors.details: Botswana retains strong leverage through its partnership with De Beers, but global synthetic diamonds and weaker demand could reduce fiscal and negotiating space.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral and water constraints
frictionVectors.details: New coal, copper, and critical-mineral projects require foreign capital while water scarcity limits industrial expansion. The government is seeking investment without surrendering regulatory control.

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: Authorities are pursuing greater state participation and tighter oversight of industrial and artisanal gold production. This improves formal sovereign control but risks deterring investors and increasing opaque trade.

frictionVectors.title: Security dependence on Russia
frictionVectors.details: The government's reliance on Russian-linked security support reduces Western influence but creates new dependency risks involving mining access, arms, and political alignment.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concessions and Foreign Capital
frictionVectors.details: Burundi is seeking investment in nickel and other minerals, but weak regulatory capacity leaves the state exposed to opaque contracts and limited local value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Regional Security Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Tensions involving Rwanda and armed activity around the eastern Great Lakes constrain government resources and increase reliance on external security and diplomatic partners.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Maritime Infrastructure Competition
frictionVectors.details: Cabo Verde's ports and maritime position attract competing European, Chinese, and wider Atlantic interests, creating leverage but also dependency risks.

frictionVectors.title: Tourism and Energy Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Heavy reliance on imported energy, tourism, and external financing limits domestic control over critical economic infrastructure despite strong institutions.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese Infrastructure and Resource Access
frictionVectors.details: Chinese financing and construction remain important for roads, ports, and extractive projects, while repayment and concession structures can reduce policy flexibility.

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone Conflict and Resource Corridors
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in the Northwest and Southwest disrupts transport, agriculture, and local resource governance, while insecurity also affects cross-border trade and energy planning.

frictionVectors.title: Gold and Diamond Concessions
frictionVectors.details: Foreign security-linked actors and domestic elites compete for access to gold and diamonds, with weak oversight limiting public revenue and local control.

frictionVectors.title: Dependence on External Security Guarantees
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on Russian-linked forces and other outside partners strengthens regime survival but narrows sovereign decision-making and complicates relations with Western and regional institutions.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Sector Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chad's fiscal position and external leverage remain tied to oil production and export infrastructure, with limited diversification or domestic processing capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Post-French Security Realignment
frictionVectors.details: The recalibration of French military ties creates space for new regional and extra-regional partners, but persistent insecurity constrains independent control over borders and strategic corridors.

highlights: External financing fills domestic capacity gaps

frictionVectors.title: Mayotte and maritime jurisdiction
frictionVectors.details: The unresolved dispute with France over Mayotte limits Comoros's effective control of surrounding maritime space and complicates migration and fisheries policy.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Roads, ports, energy, and telecommunications remain reliant on external donors and contractors, leaving limited national leverage over strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals bargaining imbalance
frictionVectors.details: Foreign firms and trading networks retain substantial influence over copper and cobalt finance, processing, and export chains, despite Kinshasa's efforts to renegotiate terms.

frictionVectors.title: M23 and regional security competition
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in the east, including alleged external support to armed actors, weakens state control over mining corridors and increases dependence on regional and international security partners.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon concentration
frictionVectors.details: The economy remains heavily dependent on offshore oil and foreign operators, limiting diversification and exposing national revenue to external commercial and price pressures.

frictionVectors.title: Port and debt exposure
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-financed transport infrastructure, including the Pointe-Noire corridor, provides connectivity but narrows fiscal room and can give creditors influence over strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa-chain dependency
frictionVectors.details: Côte d'Ivoire has strengthened producer governance and local processing, but foreign traders, lenders, and manufacturers still capture much of the value and shape market access.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic infrastructure competition
frictionVectors.details: Port, rail, energy, and digital projects attract French, Chinese, and Gulf-backed capital, creating growth opportunities while increasing competition for influence over national logistics.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-base dependence
frictionVectors.details: The concentration of foreign military facilities gives Djibouti substantial rental income and diplomatic leverage, but also constrains independent security choices and deepens great-power competition.

frictionVectors.title: Port and debt exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed port and logistics infrastructure has expanded national connectivity while leaving Djibouti vulnerable to debt pressure, commercial disputes, and external control over strategic corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Gulf Capital and State-Asset Sales
frictionVectors.details: Heavy external financing needs are increasing Gulf and international leverage over strategic land, ports, and state-linked assets. Cairo retains formal control but is trading portions of economic sovereignty for liquidity.

frictionVectors.title: Nile Water and Red Sea Exposure
frictionVectors.details: The GERD dispute and instability around the Red Sea threaten Egypt's water security and maritime revenues. Suez remains a major strategic asset, but regional conflict can rapidly reduce its returns.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Depletion
frictionVectors.details: Declining oil and gas output is narrowing fiscal space and increasing dependence on foreign operators, technical partners, and new offshore investment. The state retains ownership, but operational capacity and revenue resilience are weakening.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Malabo's infrastructure ambitions rely heavily on external contractors and commodity-linked financing. Strategic facilities can provide leverage, but low utilization and opaque contracting limit broad sovereign gains.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea Militarization
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's coastline gives it strategic value as outside powers compete for access and influence around the Red Sea. Asmara seeks to avoid dependence while using geopolitical competition to preserve regime autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Mining Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Gold and other mineral projects provide hard currency but depend on foreign capital, technology, and offtake arrangements. Limited transparency and sanctions risk constrain the state's ability to convert resources into durable national capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Dependence on South African Corridors
frictionVectors.details: Trade, energy supply, logistics, and labor links with South Africa provide essential access but leave Eswatini vulnerable to decisions made beyond its borders. SACU revenues remain a critical buffer against this structural dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Investment Access Versus Political Reform
frictionVectors.details: Foreign investors seek predictable infrastructure and industrial policy while political restrictions continue to generate reputational and diplomatic pressure. The resulting uncertainty limits diversification beyond sugar, textiles, and state-linked projects.

frictionVectors.title: Nile Dam Diplomacy
frictionVectors.details: The GERD strengthens Ethiopia's control over its electricity strategy and regional bargaining position, but unresolved tensions with Egypt and Sudan keep water infrastructure politically exposed. Seasonal filling and dam operations remain potential escalation points.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Port-Access Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and the search for dependable maritime access are drawing Ethiopia toward competing Gulf, Chinese, Western, and regional partners. External financing can accelerate infrastructure delivery while narrowing policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: France Relationship Reset
frictionVectors.details: Libreville is seeking greater autonomy from traditional French political, security, and commercial networks while avoiding disruption to critical investment and expertise.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Gabon remains dependent on foreign capital and operators for manganese, oil, rail, and port infrastructure, limiting the state’s ability to capture full resource value.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Fisheries Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Weak monitoring capacity leaves Gambian waters vulnerable to illegal, underreported, and foreign-linked fishing, reducing public returns from marine resources.

frictionVectors.title: Regional Logistics Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia’s trade and food security remain closely tied to Senegalese transit routes and regional infrastructure, creating exposure to cross-border political or commercial disputes.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal Mining and Water Stress
frictionVectors.details: Unregulated gold mining continues to damage farmland and water systems while complicating efforts to formalize artisanal production and retain more value domestically.

frictionVectors.title: IMF and Creditor Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and IMF-linked fiscal discipline constrain policy space over energy, mining, and state-owned infrastructure, even as Accra seeks stronger local-content rules.

frictionVectors.title: Simandou Consortium Bargaining
frictionVectors.details: The state is attempting to convert the Simandou iron-ore project into rail, port, and industrial benefits, but its negotiating position is balanced against powerful foreign mining consortia.

frictionVectors.title: Transition Legitimacy Crisis
frictionVectors.details: Military rule and uncertainty over a return to constitutional government increase sanctions risk and make long-term resource contracts vulnerable to political renegotiation.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Cashew Chains
frictionVectors.details: External traders and processors capture much of the value from Guinea-Bissau’s dominant cashew sector, leaving producers exposed to price swings and limited domestic processing.

frictionVectors.title: Cocaine and Port Governance
frictionVectors.details: Transnational narcotics networks exploit weak institutions and maritime access, undermining customs authority and making infrastructure investment vulnerable to political capture.

frictionVectors.title: External debt and infrastructure leverage
frictionVectors.details: Kenya is balancing IMF-linked fiscal reforms against repayment obligations and infrastructure relationships involving China and other external lenders. Budget pressure limits Nairobi's room to renegotiate major projects on purely sovereign terms.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: The Lamu and Mombasa corridors remain exposed to regional insecurity and competition from Tanzanian and Djiboutian routes. Oil, logistics, and naval access give outside partners continuing influence over coastal infrastructure.

highlights: Polihali project deepens South African dependence

frictionVectors.title: Lesotho Highlands Water Project
frictionVectors.details: Water revenues and dam construction are strategically vital but bind Lesotho's fiscal and infrastructure outlook to South Africa. Delays, cost escalation, and unequal bargaining power remain persistent sovereignty concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Textile and labor vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: The export-manufacturing base remains highly dependent on external trade preferences and foreign-owned supply chains. Changes in United States or regional market access can rapidly affect employment and political stability.

frictionVectors.title: ArcelorMittal and iron-ore dependence
frictionVectors.details: Iron-ore exports and rail access are dominated by concession arrangements with foreign investors, limiting Liberia's ability to capture value beyond royalties and jobs. Expansion of mining corridors will intensify disputes over land, taxes, and local benefits.

frictionVectors.title: Freeport of Monrovia influence
frictionVectors.details: The port is central to national revenue and regional trade, while foreign operators and partners retain substantial commercial leverage. Security, customs modernization, and concession terms remain sensitive sovereignty issues.

highlights: Foreign patrons shape the security map

frictionVectors.title: Competing control over oil institutions
frictionVectors.details: Rival political and armed networks continue to contest access to production, export terminals, and national revenue flows. International energy companies operate under substantial political and security uncertainty.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign military and mercenary presence
frictionVectors.details: External powers support opposing Libyan actors through military, financial, and diplomatic channels. This reduces Tripoli's and eastern authorities' independent control over strategic bases, borders, and energy infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Nickel, cobalt, and mineral concessions
frictionVectors.details: Large mining projects such as Ambatovy and other resource ventures bring foreign capital but expose Madagascar to volatile prices, tax disputes, and environmental conflict. Domestic processing and state revenue capture remain limited.

frictionVectors.title: QMM and coastal infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: The ilmenite operation and associated port infrastructure in the southeast remain flashpoints over land rights, water access, compensation, and environmental damage. Weak transport connectivity increases investor leverage over project logistics.

frictionVectors.title: External Debt and Fiscal Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and reliance on IMF and bilateral creditors limit Malawi's room to direct foreign exchange, energy, and development policy independently.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals and Power Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Renewed interest in uranium and other mineral projects could expand revenues, but weak electricity and transport infrastructure leave bargaining power tilted toward external investors.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The military government has reduced Western engagement while relying increasingly on Russian security support, creating new strategic dependence amid persistent jihadist violence.

frictionVectors.title: Gold Mining Control
frictionVectors.details: Bamako is seeking a larger share of gold revenues and tighter oversight of foreign operators, but opaque contracting, sanctions exposure, and insecurity complicate effective sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: GTA Gas Project Governance
frictionVectors.details: The offshore Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project with Senegal offers new fiscal and diplomatic leverage, but cross-border revenue management and foreign-operated infrastructure remain sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Iron Ore and Chinese Influence
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore exports and transport corridors remain central to the economy, leaving Mauritania exposed to commodity cycles and dependent on external capital, including Chinese participation.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos and Diego Garcia
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius's sovereignty claim over the Chagos Archipelago remains strategically important, with the future of the Diego Garcia base requiring delicate negotiation with the United Kingdom and United States.

frictionVectors.title: External Financial and Maritime Exposure
frictionVectors.details: The economy depends heavily on foreign finance, tourism, and maritime services, while India, China, and Western partners compete for influence over ports, digital infrastructure, and the ocean economy.

highlights: Western Sahara remains the core contest

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara Resource Diplomacy
frictionVectors.details: Morocco uses phosphate, fisheries, ports, and renewable-energy development in Western Sahara to reinforce its territorial claim, provoking legal and diplomatic resistance from Algeria and the Polisario Front.

frictionVectors.title: Competing External Partnerships
frictionVectors.details: Deepening ties with the European Union, United States, Gulf states, and China bring investment and technology but require Rabat to balance divergent expectations over security, infrastructure, and market access.

highlights: Cabo Delgado Remains the Sovereignty Test

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Led LNG Security and Ownership
frictionVectors.details: Large offshore gas projects remain dependent on international operators, lenders, and security support. Insurgency in Cabo Delgado limits Maputo's effective control over the resource zone and delays revenue realization.

frictionVectors.title: Northern Transport Corridors
frictionVectors.details: Road, port, and logistics infrastructure around Palma and Pemba is strategically important but vulnerable to conflict disruption. External investment is strengthening connectivity while increasing dependence on foreign capital and contractors.

highlights: Oil and Green Hydrogen Raise Strategic Stakes

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Oil Licensing and Revenue Control
frictionVectors.details: Recent petroleum prospects have intensified competition among international firms and raised expectations for stricter local-content and revenue rules. Namibia is seeking investment without surrendering excessive control over emerging offshore assets.

frictionVectors.title: Green Hydrogen Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Hydrogen projects require large external financing, export infrastructure, and technology partnerships. This creates a risk that Namibia captures limited domestic value unless ownership, power access, and industrial processing are tightly regulated.

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Mining Renegotiations
frictionVectors.details: Niamey is pushing for greater state control and revised terms in uranium and other extractive sectors. The shift improves formal sovereignty but risks lower investment, revenue disruption, and prolonged disputes with foreign operators.

frictionVectors.title: Russian and Regional Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Reduced Western security cooperation has increased reliance on alternative external partners and regional alliances. This may preserve regime autonomy while exposing infrastructure and mining areas to weak oversight and security volatility.

highlights: Oil Wealth Still Leaks Through Insecurity

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline Theft and Niger Delta Control
frictionVectors.details: Crude theft, sabotage, and local grievances continue to reduce state capture of petroleum value. Domestic refining capacity offers greater leverage, but supply reliability and pipeline governance remain weak.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capital and Critical Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Nigeria still depends on international finance, technology, and operators across oil, gas, power, and transport. Abuja is seeking stronger local participation while balancing investment needs against concerns over opaque contracts and strategic dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern Congo Mineral Supply Chains
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's role in regional mineral trading remains closely scrutinized amid allegations that conflict-linked supply chains pass through its territory. International pressure could affect export access, sanctions exposure, and Kigali's broader sovereignty strategy.

frictionVectors.title: Donor and Security Partnership Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda retains strong administrative control but remains exposed to external aid, investment, and security relationships. Shifts in donor tolerance over regional military activity could constrain policy autonomy and infrastructure financing.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Hydrocarbon Dependence
frictionVectors.details: São Tomé and Príncipe remains dependent on foreign technical and financial partners to evaluate offshore petroleum prospects. Unproven reserves limit bargaining power while exploration terms could shape long-term sovereignty over maritime resources.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Fisheries
frictionVectors.details: Limited enforcement capacity leaves the country's tuna and other marine resources exposed to foreign fleets and unequal licensing arrangements. Maritime surveillance and port infrastructure remain inadequate.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Energy Contract Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking greater local value capture and tighter oversight of projects involving international operators such as Woodside, BP, and Kosmos. Renegotiation risks investor uncertainty and delays in developing the Sangomar and GTA fields.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure and Debt Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Transport, power, and port expansion depend heavily on external finance and contractors, including Chinese and Gulf-linked capital. High debt-service pressures could narrow Dakar's room to direct future resource revenues toward domestic development.

frictionVectors.title: Tuna Access and Maritime Control
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles captures important revenue from foreign tuna fleets but has limited capacity to monitor its vast maritime zone. Tensions persist between licensing income, conservation requirements, and demands for greater local processing.

frictionVectors.title: External Security and Infrastructure Reliance
frictionVectors.details: The islands rely on partners including India, France, and other external actors for maritime surveillance, port support, and strategic infrastructure. This improves security but creates sensitivity over foreign military access and long-term dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Mining Dominance
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, rutile, and bauxite development remains dependent on foreign capital and operators, with recurring disputes over taxes, licenses, labor conditions, and environmental impacts. The state has increased scrutiny but still captures limited value beyond royalties and employment.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese-Linked Logistics Influence
frictionVectors.details: Mining corridors, rail connections, and port infrastructure are closely tied to external investors and contractors, particularly from China. Concentration of control over export routes could constrain Freetown's negotiating leverage and deepen commodity dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Security and Port Competition
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, and other external actors retain significant influence through military cooperation, port relationships, and support to competing Somali authorities. This complicates federal control over ports, customs, and maritime resources.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Oil and Fisheries Governance
frictionVectors.details: Prospective offshore hydrocarbons and valuable fisheries are being developed amid weak enforcement and unresolved federal-regional authority disputes. Foreign operators and fleets may gain access faster than Somalia builds transparent licensing, environmental safeguards, and maritime protection.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral Processing and Foreign Capital
frictionVectors.details: South Africa retains major platinum-group, manganese, and chrome assets, but limited domestic processing leaves leverage dispersed among multinational buyers and investors. Competition among China, the United States, and the European Union is intensifying around critical-minerals supply chains.

frictionVectors.title: Power, Rail, and Port Constraints
frictionVectors.details: Electricity reliability and freight bottlenecks continue to weaken state control over strategic infrastructure and constrain mineral exports. Private-sector participation is expanding, but raises concerns over regulatory capacity and long-term public ownership.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline Dependence on Sudan
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan remains dependent on pipelines and export infrastructure crossing Sudan, exposing its main revenue stream to war-related disruption and bargaining pressure. The arrangement limits independent control over production, transport, and marketing.

frictionVectors.title: Elite and External Control of Oil
frictionVectors.details: Oil revenues remain concentrated among political elites and external operators while fiscal institutions and oversight stay weak. Chinese and regional commercial interests retain significant influence over production and infrastructure decisions.

frictionVectors.title: Externalization of the Gold Economy
frictionVectors.details: Gold production and export networks help finance competing armed actors and are vulnerable to smuggling and foreign brokerage. Regional powers and private intermediaries can obtain influence without strengthening Sudanese state institutions.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea Infrastructure Contest
frictionVectors.details: Port access and military-logistics interests around the Red Sea remain entangled with Sudan's civil war and competing external relationships. Fragmented authority makes long-term control of transport, energy, and mineral infrastructure highly uncertain.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Corridor Concessions
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is expanding ports, railways, and trade corridors to strengthen its position as an inland gateway, including through foreign-backed concessions and financing. These projects improve connectivity but create debate over transparency, debt exposure, and sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: LNG and Critical-Minerals Bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Prospective gas development and rising interest in graphite and other minerals give Dar es Salaam greater negotiating leverage. Delays, local-content demands, and competition among Asian, Western, and Gulf investors continue to shape the terms of extraction.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Influence at the Port
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Lomé strengthens Togo's regional trade position but depends heavily on foreign shipping, finance, and logistics capital. This creates revenue opportunities while limiting fully autonomous control over strategic transport infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Northern Border Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Instability spreading southward from the Sahel raises costs for roads, border logistics, and northern resource access. Security partnerships and external assistance may improve resilience but can also deepen foreign influence over internal security priorities.

frictionVectors.title: EU MIGRATION-ENERGY BARGAIN
frictionVectors.details: European financial and political support remains linked to migration control, creating leverage over Tunisian policy. Tunisia is also seeking external capital for energy imports and renewable projects.

frictionVectors.title: PHOSPHATE SECTOR STAGNATION
frictionVectors.details: Production and export capacity remain below potential because of infrastructure, labor, and governance constraints. This limits Tunisia's ability to convert mineral resources into stronger fiscal sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP FINANCING AND SANCTIONS
frictionVectors.details: The oil pipeline remains central to Uganda's resource strategy but faces sustained environmental criticism, financing constraints, and Western political pressure. Dependence on foreign partners for construction, transport, and markets limits domestic control over the value chain.

frictionVectors.title: CHINESE INFRASTRUCTURE DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Chinese contractors and lenders retain a major role in transport and energy infrastructure. These projects improve connectivity while increasing long-term exposure to external financing and procurement conditions.

frictionVectors.title: COPPER OWNERSHIP AND VALUE ADDITION
frictionVectors.details: Zambia is pressing for greater fiscal returns, local processing, and supply-chain participation as global demand for critical minerals rises. Foreign mining capital remains indispensable, limiting the government's bargaining room.

frictionVectors.title: MULTIPLE EXTERNAL FINANCIAL CENTERS
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and investment negotiations involve China, Western creditors, and multilateral institutions. Improved access to finance could strengthen sovereignty, but reform conditions and repayment obligations remain significant constraints.

frictionVectors.title: LITHIUM EXPORT-CONTROL PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: Zimbabwe is attempting to retain more value from lithium and other critical minerals through export restrictions and processing ambitions. Limited domestic capital, technology, and reliable power leave the sector dependent on foreign operators.

frictionVectors.title: SANCTIONS, MINING FINANCE, AND ELITE CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: Sanctions, currency instability, and governance concerns raise the cost of infrastructure and mining finance. Resource rents remain vulnerable to opaque state-business networks and external firms able to access hard currency.
